introduction: Imogen, daughter of Britain's King Cymbeline, has married the gentleman Posthumus against her father's wishes. His banishment leaves her exposed to a hostile stepmother and an unwelcome royal suitor, while separation draws their loyalty into a dangerous wager abroad. At the same time, Britain moves toward conflict with Rome, and two lost princes grow up far from court. Disguises, stolen tokens and mistaken judgments connect private love with questions of inheritance, service and the power to forgive.

fullSynopsis.text: Cymbeline, King of Britain, has banished Posthumus Leonatus for marrying his daughter Imogen, whom he intended for his Queen's son Cloten. The lovers exchange a ring and bracelet before separating. In Rome, Posthumus defends Imogen's fidelity so confidently that he wagers her ring against Iachimo's money on the Italian's failure to seduce her. Iachimo reaches Britain with letters of introduction and invents tales of Posthumus's infidelity, offering himself as revenge. Imogen angrily rejects him. He retreats into an apology, then persuades her to store a trunk supposedly containing valuables in her bedchamber.

The Queen plots to secure the succession for Cloten and gives Pisanio, Posthumus's faithful servant, what she presents as medicine but believes is poison. The suspicious physician Cornelius has substituted a drug that only imitates death. Meanwhile, Iachimo emerges from the trunk while Imogen sleeps, steals her bracelet and notes the room and a distinctive mole on her breast. Back in Rome, these details overcome Posthumus's initial doubts and Philario's objections. Believing adultery proved, Posthumus gives up the ring and turns his anguish into violent condemnation of women. Cloten's unwanted courtship has separately driven Imogen to proclaim Posthumus's poorest garment dearer than Cloten himself.

Cymbeline refuses Rome's demand for tribute, supported by the Queen and Cloten, and war follows. Posthumus orders Pisanio to kill Imogen, luring her toward Milford Haven with a promised reunion. Pisanio instead shows her the command, refuses murder and proposes to report her dead while she disguises herself as a boy to seek Roman service. He gives her the Queen's supposed restorative. Cloten forces Pisanio to reveal the destination and supply Posthumus's clothes, intending to murder the husband and rape Imogen in them. Elsewhere in Wales, the exiled Belarius secretly raises Cymbeline's stolen sons as his own, under the names Polydore and Cadwal.

Calling herself Fidele, Imogen finds food and kindness in Belarius's cave, unaware that his young companions are her brothers Guiderius and Arviragus. When illness leads her to take the drug, they discover her apparently dead and prepare funeral honours. Meanwhile, Cloten encounters Guiderius, threatens him and is killed in their fight. His headless body, still wearing Posthumus's clothes, is laid beside Fidele. Imogen wakes and mistakes it for her husband, blaming Pisanio for treachery. Lucius, the Roman commander, finds the grieving page and takes Fidele into his service. Belarius reluctantly follows the brothers when they insist on fighting for Britain.

Posthumus arrives with the Roman forces, carrying the bloody token that makes him believe Imogen has been killed. Repenting his command even before discovering her innocence, he dresses as a British peasant and fights against the army with which he came. He defeats Iachimo, then joins Belarius and the princes in rescuing Cymbeline and rallying the retreating Britons. After victory he seeks death by presenting himself as a Roman prisoner. As he sleeps in prison, his dead family appear to petition Jupiter, who descends with a promise of deliverance and a prophetic tablet. Posthumus wakes to find its mysterious writing.

At Cymbeline's tent, Cornelius reports the Queen's death and her confession of plans to poison Imogen and the King. Lucius asks mercy for Fidele, who instead uses a royal boon to question Iachimo about the ring. His confession exposes the deception. Posthumus identifies himself and confesses ordering Imogen's death, then strikes the page who interrupts him. Pisanio reveals her identity, and Cornelius explains the sleeping drug. Imogen and Posthumus embrace. Guiderius admits killing Cloten and faces punishment until Belarius discloses that he and Arviragus are Cymbeline's lost sons; their identity is supported by a birthmark and Belarius's offer to produce a preserved mantle.

The King welcomes his children and restores Belarius to favour. Posthumus reveals that he was the unknown soldier who helped save Britain and pardons the kneeling Iachimo, who offers back ring and bracelet. Cymbeline extends pardon to all the prisoners. The soothsayer interprets Jupiter's prophecy through the lovers' reunion and the princes' return. Although victorious, Cymbeline agrees to resume Rome's tribute, blaming the Queen's influence for its refusal. British and Roman standards are to march together as the reunited court prepares sacrifices, public peace and celebration.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Courtiers explain that Cymbeline has lost two sons to childhood theft and now rejects his remaining child's marriage to Posthumus, preferring the Queen's son Cloten. Imogen and the banished Posthumus exchange tokens before their enforced separation; Pisanio remains to serve her. Cloten's frustrated pursuit contrasts with the couple's affection. In Rome, Iachimo challenges Posthumus's praise of Imogen's chastity and wagers money against her ring that he can win her. In Britain, the Queen obtains supposed poisons and gives a box to Pisanio as a restorative, intending harm to him and Imogen. Cornelius reveals that he has secretly substituted a harmless drug producing temporary apparent death. Iachimo claims Posthumus is unfaithful and offers himself to Imogen, but her rejection forces him to pretend he was merely testing her loyalty. He then obtains permission to leave a supposedly valuable trunk in her chamber overnight.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Cloten's boasting and crude behaviour expose the foolishness behind his rank. In Imogen's chamber, Iachimo secretly emerges from the trunk, records its furnishings, removes her bracelet and observes a mole on her breast as fabricated proof of intimacy. He returns to hiding without her waking. Cloten then serenades Imogen and persists in his suit, relying on royal support. She rejects him decisively, declaring even Posthumus's meanest garment more valuable to her; the phrase fuels his resentment. She also discovers that her bracelet is missing. In Rome, Iachimo claims victory in the wager. Posthumus initially dismisses descriptions of the chamber and briefly accepts Philario's suggestion that the bracelet might have been stolen. Iachimo's oath and knowledge of the mole overwhelm these doubts. Posthumus surrenders the ring, imagines Imogen's betrayal as certain and expands his anger into a denunciation of all women.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Cymbeline rejects Rome's demand for tribute and prepares for war. Posthumus sends Pisanio an order to kill Imogen, using a loving letter to draw her toward Milford Haven. In Wales, Belarius describes his exile while the young men he calls his sons yearn for wider experience; alone, he reveals that they are Cymbeline's stolen princes. Pisanio tells Imogen the truth and refuses to kill her. He plans to satisfy Posthumus with a false report of death, while she assumes male disguise and seeks service with Lucius. He gives her the Queen's supposed medicine. At court, Cloten coerces Pisanio into supplying the letter and Posthumus's clothes, planning murder and rape in revenge for her insult. Imogen, now Fidele, loses her way and finds hospitality with Belarius, Guiderius and Arviragus, who feel an immediate affection for her. Rome raises forces for the invasion.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Cloten reaches Wales dressed as Posthumus and intent on violence. Imogen feels ill and takes the supposed restorative before remaining behind at the cave. Cloten encounters Guiderius, exchanges threats and fights him; Guiderius returns with his severed head. Belarius fears the consequences of killing the Queen's son. Arviragus then brings out Fidele apparently dead, and the brothers honour the beloved stranger with a funeral song. They lay Cloten's body nearby. Imogen wakes and, recognizing Posthumus's garments on the headless corpse, mistakenly concludes that Pisanio and Cloten murdered her husband. Lucius finds her in grief and accepts Fidele as his page. Meanwhile, Cymbeline faces invasion with his daughter and Cloten missing and the Queen dangerously ill. Pisanio knows neither Imogen's whereabouts nor Cloten's fate. Guiderius and Arviragus reject Belarius's plan to hide from the war and persuade him to join their service to Britain.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Believing Imogen dead, Posthumus repents his murderous command and fights disguised for Britain. He and Belarius's household rescue Cymbeline and turn defeat into victory. Posthumus then submits as a Roman prisoner, hoping for death. In a prison vision his family petition Jupiter, who promises restoration and leaves a prophetic tablet. At court, Cornelius reports the Queen's death and murderous plans. Fidele's question about the ring elicits Iachimo's confession. Posthumus reveals his identity, strikes the intervening page, then discovers Imogen alive; the drug's true effect clears Pisanio. Guiderius's admission that he killed Cloten brings a death sentence, but Belarius reveals the princes' identities and his own role in their theft. The family reunites, Belarius is forgiven and Posthumus pardons Iachimo. The soothsayer explains the prophecy, and Cymbeline pardons the prisoners and restores tribute to Rome, choosing reconciliation despite British victory.
